paragraphs.text: Smart Office with a Micro:bit Hub

paragraphs.name: ce54
paragraphs.text: The simple task of making a complicated project.

paragraphs.name: a6d1
paragraphs.text: Editor’s note: James is 12 at time of writing, and already a pretty amazing coder! That’s about all the context you need for this piece.

paragraphs.name: 7e77
paragraphs.text: Before I joined Tinkertanker as an intern, I had some experience with Node.js and APIs. So when YJ asked me to do a project with the micro:bit, my first (and only) thought was… why not hook micro:bits to APIs?

paragraphs.name: 521c
paragraphs.text: After brainstorming for a short while, I decided to create a micro:bit “hub” system for the office, where multiple micro:bits feed (using the built-in radio functionality) to the main micro:bit “hub”, which writes to serial for a computer running a Node.js script to read. Seems pretty simple, right?

paragraphs.name: 8acb
paragraphs.text: The API I decided to work with was Slack, which is Tinkertanker’s office chat platform for staff and interns. Thank you, Slack, for having a very well documented API, I’d give you a cookie if I had any 🍪

paragraphs.name: b840
paragraphs.text: TRYING
On to business. I wired up a motion sensor to the micro:bit, placed it near the office entrance, and got the microbit to send a string as a radio signal:

paragraphs.name: 4e45
paragraphs.text: Simple, eh?

paragraphs.name: b91f
paragraphs.text: Notice something? Yes, that’s a JSON string!

paragraphs.name: 4c31
paragraphs.text: I decided that the the Node.js program receiving the signal would JSON.parse()the JSON, and respond accordingly.

paragraphs.name: af53
paragraphs.text: As the radio signal couldn’t reach the computer hosting the Node code, I set up another micro:bit to serve as a “hub”, then programmed the “hub” to relay signals through serial:
This version of the “Hub” is newer, but still compatible

paragraphs.name: 8e5c
paragraphs.text: Also a newer version of the package.json file

paragraphs.name: cb28
paragraphs.text: Then, on to my favorite part, Node.js. Here are the modules I used:

paragraphs.name: cddb
paragraphs.text: node-fetch, to use HTTP requests in Node

paragraphs.name: 0b2f
paragraphs.text: serialport, to, unsurprisingly, access serial ports

paragraphs.name: ffc8
paragraphs.text: Express, a web framework for Node

paragraphs.name: 24a4
paragraphs.text: Serialport had an convenient on(‘data’) event, which I happily used… except that I got buffers as data.

paragraphs.name: 2dcc
paragraphs.text: Good thing you can break buffers back down into strings, right? Look what that got me….

paragraphs.name: 4eb6
paragraphs.text: I was about to just do some interesting technique to solve this when I realised, hey, there’s a serialport parser!

paragraphs.name: f160
paragraphs.text: True enough, I could add in the parser to read the data as a whole string!

paragraphs.name: 2c1d
paragraphs.text: var SerialPort = require('serialport');
const Readline = require('@serialport/parser-readline')

paragraphs.name: 31c6
paragraphs.text: var port = new SerialPort('/dev/cu.usbmodem1412', {

paragraphs.name: 5cb8
paragraphs.text: baudRate: 115200
const parser = port.pipe(new Readline({ delimiter: '\r\n' }))

paragraphs.name: 9a94
paragraphs.text: Yes! Everything was working perfectly. Now to JSON.parse(data)!

paragraphs.name: 2e69
paragraphs.text: Much to my dismay, the string didn’t happen to be a valid JSON. How, then? When I console.log(data) ed it, it produced a seemingly valid string of JSON. (That’s when YJ Soon came in and spotted a programming error: data.trim instead of data.trim, what a careless mistake!)

paragraphs.name: 96ea
paragraphs.text: So, I was almost done, now to send a message in Slack! I wrote the following code for that.

let json = `{"attachments":[{"fallback":"Someone entered/exited", "title":"Someone entered/exited", "callback_id": "motiondetect", "color": "#add8e6", "attachment_type": "default", "actions": [{"name":"who","text":"It was me", "type": "button", "value": "me"}]}]}`

paragraphs.name: ef11
paragraphs.text:
fetch('https://hooks.slack.com/services/...',
{ method: 'POST',
  body: json,
  headers: {'Content-type': "application/json"}}).catch()

paragraphs.name: c40c
paragraphs.text: Spammy, Spammy, Ham

paragraphs.name: b145
paragraphs.text: And I got that message in Slack. Quite a few times, because we had so many people walking in and out. But still, I got that message.

paragraphs.name: bbd8
paragraphs.text: Wondering why I had Express as a dependency? I actually also made a quick website to serve staff at Tinkertanker with the latest feeds from sensors.

paragraphs.name: 8af7
paragraphs.text: After that it worked perfectly. So happily ever after! (Until I decided to expand the whole system and also remove that micro:bit 😏)
